title: Kairos: The Right Moment
short: Kairos is the fitting moment: an argument works when it suits its time, place and audience.
trouble: Learners ignore timing. The same words can persuade one week and fall flat the next.

blocks.html: The Greeks had two words for time. Chronos is clock time. Kairos is the right time: the fitting moment to speak, and the fitting thing to say at that moment. Teachers of rhetoric from the 400s BC on taught that an argument works only when it suits its occasion. Kairos adds the clock and the calendar to the appeals you have been identifying.

blocks.name: wr-triangle
blocks.cap: Kairos lives in the context around the triangle: time, place and occasion.

blocks.html: Kairos is the fitting moment. Ask: why this argument now, here, to this audience? A writer can wait for the right moment, or show readers why the moment has come.

Audiences listen when the issue is on their minds. A request for a crosswalk lands better the week after a near miss than in a quiet month, and a speech about liberty means more on Independence Day. The words may be the same; the moment changes what they can do.

blocks.title: Douglass names the moment
blocks.q: Douglass, July 5, 1852: “At a time like this, scorching irony, not convincing argument, is needed.” How does he use kairos?
steps: He was invited to speak about the Fourth of July, a day for celebrating liberty.
He says the moment calls for a certain kind of speech: irony and rebuke, not a calm proof that slavery is wrong. His audience already knew it was wrong.
The holiday itself becomes his argument: “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?”
blocks.a: He turns the occasion into his subject and says outright what the moment demands.

blocks.title: Everyday kairos
blocks.q: A student wants the cafeteria to add a salad bar. When should she send her proposal: (A) in May, when the menu committee plans next year’s food; (B) in October, after the menu is set; (C) whenever she finishes it?
steps: The audience can act on the request only when it is making decisions.
In May the committee is choosing next year’s menu. In October its choices are made.
If she must write in October, she can still use kairos by asking to be on May’s agenda.
blocks.a: A: send it when the audience can act on it.

blocks.html: Ignoring timing. The same words can persuade one week and fall flat the next: a joke during a crisis, a request after the budget is decided, a long speech after a long program. Check: what just happened that your reader is thinking about? Connect your claim to it, or wait for a better moment.

cards.text: Proposing a later start time at the board meeting where next year’s calendar is voted on.
Asking for a bigger field-trip budget the day after the budget was approved.
cards.why: The decision has already been made.

cards.text: Writing to the paper about a dangerous corner the week after a near miss there.
Telling a funny story to open a speech at a memorial service.
cards.why: The occasion calls for a different tone.

cards.text: Asking neighbors to join a park cleanup on Earth Day weekend.
cards.why: The date gives people a reason to act now.
